narrative:
The model estimated an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is a high-risk prediction, not a certainty, but it is the reason your application was denied: the admissions decision treated this risk score as a decisive concern about your ability to meet the program’s bar-passage expectations. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The strongest factor was your third-year class decile. You are in decile 1, while accepted students average about 5.79; this comparatively weak third-year academic standing pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 24.5, well below the accepted-student average of about 37.18; this also pushed toward failure. Third was your first-year class decile. At 1 versus an accepted average of 6.00, it added further weight toward the same conclusion. Together, these three academic indicators—especially your third-year standing and LSAT—drove the denial.

To improve your chances, ask admissions whether a reconsideration process exists and what evidence they would accept. Plan to retake the LSAT with structured preparation and aim for a substantially higher score. Also consider strengthening your academic record through additional relevant coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, and apply to schools with more flexible admission profiles. A personal statement or addendum explaining your preparation and demonstrated improvement could help, but it should be supported by concrete new academic evidence.
